title: Musk and Intel Break Ground on $16.8B Terafab, US-China AI Tensions Escalate Ahead of Xi-Trump Summit
subhead: SpaceX, Tesla, xAI and Intel confirm the world's largest chip fab in Texas at $16.8B, while Beijing and Washington trade accusations over AI model IP theft and potential bans ahead of a September summit. Goldman Sachs raises China AI revenue forecast to $13B.

sections.heading: Terafab Goes Live: Musk's $16.8B Chip Megafactory Lands in Texas With Intel
sections.body:
SpaceX and Tesla confirmed Thursday a joint venture with xAI and Intel Corp. to build Terafab, a semiconductor manufacturing campus in Grimes County, Texas, with an initial investment of $16.8 billion — well below SpaceX's earlier estimate of a $55 billion first phase. The facility, which Musk described as 'the most epic chip-building effort,' is designed to eventually span 100 million square feet — roughly 10 times the size of Tesla's Gigafactory Texas.

Intel's involvement is a pivotal development. The Verge reports that Intel will handle design and fabrication, bringing its foundry expertise to a project Musk has been desperate to get off the ground. Musk had previously questioned whether the chip industry could keep up with demand: 'Can someone else build these things? I mean, it's very hard to build these things,' he said on an earnings call earlier this year. Intel, which is currently building two fabs in Arizona as part of a $20 billion expansion, will now also anchor the Texas project.

The Statesman reports that Terafab secured a $30 million Texas Enterprise Fund grant and 78% tax abatements from Grimes County, which will receive $20 million annually for 35 years ($710 million total). Local residents have collected nearly 900 signatures petitioning for transparency and environmental safeguards. Construction is expected to begin immediately, with SpaceX telling county commissioners: 'We are going to get cracking.'
sections.whyItMatters: Terafab represents the largest single chip-fab investment in US history and the first major foundry project led by an AI company rather than a traditional semiconductor firm. If it delivers, it could meaningfully reshape domestic AI chip supply — but Intel's own financial and manufacturing struggles raise real execution risk.

sections.heading: US-China AI Frictions Mount Ahead of September Xi-Trump Summit
sections.body:
Ahead of President Xi Jinping's planned September visit to Washington, multiple technology disputes are intensifying between the US and China. SCMP reports that the latest flashpoint centers on Chinese AI models: the White House accused Moonshot AI of using model distillation to copy Anthropic's Claude Fable model, while Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent warned that Chinese companies conducting 'industrial-scale distillation attacks' could face sanctions or Entity List placement.

Beijing rejected the accusations, with China's commerce ministry calling them 'a typical act of AI hegemonism.' The dispute has tangible economic consequences: a Georgia Tech analysis estimates that a potential US ban on Chinese open-weight AI models could cost American businesses up to $12 billion per year, based on OpenRouter usage data showing Chinese models offering comparable performance at 30-50% of the price of proprietary alternatives.

Broader trade tensions are also escalating. The US has imposed new restrictions on advanced robotics exports and expanded its forced-labor blacklist, while disputes over optical modules and market access continue to simmer. These issues are expected to dominate the Xi-Trump summit agenda.
sections.whyItMatters: The AI model dispute represents a new frontier in US-China tech competition — moving beyond hardware export controls into intellectual property and model architecture. A ban on Chinese AI models would be unprecedented and could fragment the global AI ecosystem.

sections.heading: China's AI Firms Scale Fast: Moonshot Targets $50B Valuation, Goldman Raises Forecast
sections.body:
Moonshot AI, the Beijing-based startup behind the Kimi K3 open-weight model, is closing a funding round expected to value the company at up to $50 billion, according to SCMP sources — a dramatic jump from its $30 billion valuation just last month. The company is also dismantling its offshore structure to pursue a Hong Kong IPO as early as year-end, making it the first major Chinese AI firm to target a public listing.

Goldman Sachs raised its forecast for China's AI model market revenue by 30% to $13 billion in year-end annualised recurring revenue, citing aggressive price cuts and accelerating corporate adoption. The bank lifted projected year-end ARR for Zhipu AI to $2.5 billion and MiniMax to $1 billion. MiniMax's newly launched H3 multimodal model is priced at just 30-50% of incumbent market levels, while DeepSeek officially launched API access for its V4 Flash model, which rivals Zhipu's flagship GLM-5.2 in front-end coding.

Tencent also expanded its global AI push this week, rolling out its Hy3 model (295 billion parameters) to international developers via WorkBuddy, Tencent Design Miora and TokenHub — free of charge through August 31. Hy3 topped the global LLM usage leaderboard on OpenRouter in its launch week, according to the company.
sections.whyItMatters: Chinese AI firms are not just matching US capabilities on performance — they're dramatically undercutting on price and moving toward public markets. Moonshot's potential IPO would be a litmus test for international investor appetite in Chinese AI.

sections.heading: China Updates Chip Design IP Rules as Huawei's Ascend Architect Goes Public
sections.body:
Premier Li Qiang signed a State Council decree revising China's regulations on the protection of integrated circuit layout designs, effective October 15. SCMP reports the revision clarifies financial penalties for infringement as well as licensing, transfer and co-ownership rights, aiming to accelerate the commercialisation of new chip designs — a key move as Beijing pushes tech self-reliance under the 15th five-year plan.

The regulatory update comes as Liao Heng, chief scientist of Huawei's semiconductor business and chief architect of its Ascend AI processors, gave a rare public interview that went viral in China. Liao, a former child prodigy who entered Tsinghua University at 14 and did postdoctoral work at Princeton, described his initial scepticism about China's chipmaking capabilities and what he called the 'blind arrogance' that working abroad instilled. He said HiSilicon's track record of taping out dozens of new chips annually 'without a single failure' changed his perspective. 'Such a high hit rate shows that every team is highly qualified,' Liao said.

The combined signal — tighter IP protection plus a senior Huawei chip designer speaking openly — reflects Beijing's twin strategy: protecting domestic innovation while projecting confidence in homegrown capabilities despite US export controls.
sections.whyItMatters: China's chip design IP reform and Huawei's public-facing talent strategy are coordinated moves to strengthen the innovation ecosystem that US export controls can't directly target. The IP rule changes could also make Chinese chip designs more attractive to foreign licensees.

sections.heading: FCC Lifts 39% TV Ownership Cap, Clearing Path for Media Consolidation
sections.body:
The US Federal Communications Commission voted 2-1 to rescind the rule barring local broadcast station owners from reaching more than 39% of US TV households, replacing it with a case-by-case review process. FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said the move would help local broadcasters survive, pointing to the decline of local newspapers. The sole Democrat on the commission, Anna Gomez, called the decision illegal, arguing that only Congress can lift the cap.

The impact is already visible. In March, the FCC approved the $3.54 billion sale of Tegna to Nexstar, waiving the 39% rule — a deal that would expand Nexstar's reach to 80% of US TV households if not reversed by courts. Senate Commerce Committee Chair Ted Cruz expressed scepticism that the FCC can lift the cap without congressional authorization.

Reporters Without Borders called the decision a surrender of 'one of the last significant safeguards against excessive concentration of media ownership,' saying it 'only benefits a handful of already powerful media conglomerates.' The organization said it is evaluating legal challenges.
sections.whyItMatters: The FCC's move could trigger a wave of local TV consolidation, with Nexstar's Tegna acquisition as the first major test case. The shift from a hard cap to case-by-case review gives the FCC enormous discretionary power over media market structure.

sections.heading: Palantir Pays 1.4% Tax Rate on $1.66B Profit as Scrutiny Grows
sections.body:
A report by the Centre for International Corporate Tax Accountability and Research (CICTAR) found that Palantir Technologies paid a global effective tax rate of just 1.4% on $1.66 billion in pretax profits in 2025 — with zero US federal corporate income tax for the third consecutive year. The company's market value stands at approximately $370 billion.

Palantir has accumulated over $3.5 billion in deferred tax assets through previous losses, R&D credits and stock-based compensation deductions, which CICTAR estimates could shelter the next $16.5 billion in profits from federal tax. Outside the US, Palantir paid less than $21.7 million in income taxes globally in 2025. In the UK, its largest non-US market with $427 million in revenue, it recorded a corporate tax charge of just £2 million.

The findings come as Palantir reported Q2 revenue of $1.94 billion, up 93% year-on-year, driven largely by government contracts. Al Jazeera reports that Palantir's technology enables agencies including ICE and DHS 'to merge vast datasets, including financial, immigration, and health records, without adequate transparency or consent.' The company has also faced criticism over its strategic partnership with Israel's Ministry of Defence.
sections.whyItMatters: Palantir's tax structure illustrates how companies deeply embedded in national security infrastructure can minimize tax contributions while profiting from public contracts — a tension that could drive policy reform as governments face fiscal pressure.

sections.heading: Türkiye Tech Watch: RedNote's Data Centre Gambit and Goldman's $13B China Signal
sections.body:
Xiaohongshu (RedNote) is reportedly planning a $2.2 billion data centre in Inner Mongolia, according to SCMP — a signal that Chinese consumer platforms are building AI infrastructure at scale despite export controls. For Türkiye, the RedNote investment is relevant because Turkish social commerce platforms like Trendyol (Alibaba-owned) and local rivals are racing to integrate AI-powered recommendation and content tools. If Chinese AI models like Moonshot's Kimi K3 and Tencent's Hy3 become available at 30-50% below US alternatives, Turkish developers face a real choice between cost and compliance risk.

Goldman Sachs' revised $13 billion China AI revenue forecast also has implications for Türkiye's positioning. As Chinese models gain global adoption — Tencent's Hy3 topped the OpenRouter usage leaderboard — Ankara will face pressure to either align with Washington's restrictions or access cheaper, competitive AI tools. Türkiye's own AI sector, including firms like Peak Games and Getir's tech arm, could benefit from the price competition but would need to navigate export control risks.
sections.whyItMatters: Türkiye's AI adoption trajectory will be shaped by the same price-performance dynamics reshaping global AI markets. The availability of competitively priced Chinese models could accelerate domestic adoption — but at geopolitical cost.

bottomLine: Thursday's developments crystallise a central tension in global tech: the physical infrastructure of AI sovereignty is being built at unprecedented scale — Terafab's $16.8B commitment, China's RedNote data centre, Moonshot's $50B valuation — while the rules governing AI intellectual property and market access remain deeply contested. The Xi-Trump summit in September will be the next inflection point. Until then, companies and governments are making irreversible bets on where chips get made, whose models run, and who pays tax.
sources: SCMP, The Verge, Statesman (Austin American-Statesman), Al Jazeera, Goldman Sachs, CSIS, CICTAR, OpenRouter, Georgia Tech, Xinhua
